reviews.title: Gute Idee – aber fragwürdiges Marketing für diese Zielgruppe
reviews.text:
Finch macht zunächst einen sympathischen und durchdachten Eindruck. Gerade für Menschen, die Schwierigkeiten mit Motivation, Routinen, Prokrastination oder ihrem allgemeinen Wohlbefinden haben, kann das Konzept sehr hilfreich sein.

Umso enttäuschender finde ich die Art, wie bereits während des Onboardings versucht wird, ein Abonnement zu verkaufen. Nachdem man der App gerade mitgeteilt hat, in welchen persönlichen Bereichen man Unterstützung benötigt, erscheint ein emotional gestaltetes Angebot mit Aussagen wie „Biggest discount ever“, „One-time offer“ und schließlich sogar „Offer expires when you exit this screen!“.

Bei mir wurden 50 % Rabatt und 39,99 € pro Jahr statt 79,99 € angeboten. Der eigentliche Preis und die automatische Verlängerung werden zwar transparent genannt – das ist nicht mein Kritikpunkt. Problematisch finde ich vielmehr den künstlichen Zeitdruck und die Angst, ein angeblich einmaliges Angebot zu verlieren.

Bei einer gewöhnlichen App würde mich aggressives Paywall-Marketing bereits stören. Bei einer Self-Care-App finde ich es besonders unpassend. Zur Zielgruppe können schließlich gerade Menschen gehören, die Unterstützung bei ADHS, Ängsten, Depressionen, Impulskontrolle, Motivation oder Selbstorganisation suchen. Ausgerechnet hier sollte man meiner Meinung nach besonders verantwortungsvoll mit FOMO und psychologischem Verkaufsdruck umgehen.

Die App selbst möchte ich damit ausdrücklich nicht als unseriös bezeichnen. Das Konzept gefällt mir sogar. Die Ar

reviews.title: Long Time User Disappointed

The current DC Supergirl event is intrusive and feels like a month long commercial. On top of that, the aggressive shift toward paywalling features makes the interface feel cluttered with locked items, and the pricing for Finch Plus has skyrocketed to a point that feels unreasonable. It is disappointing to see a mental health app prioritize branded partnerships and aggressive upselling over the user experience. The app used to be incredible but now it feels like a chore to deal with. Very disappointed in the direction they’re headed. :(

reviews.title: PLEASE DON'T WASTE YOUR TIME
reviews.text:
Don't waste hours nurturing and caring for a pet on an app that can just DELETE ALL OF YOUR DATA and not be able to retrieve it. 

I had been using Finch for almost a year under the Pro subscription. The app had helped me immensely with my mental health and organization around my home. 

Then one day when opening the app I get a message saying that my data has been corrupted. I contacted Finch's customer service and guess what their best offer was? Providing me with a coded list of all their inventory and saying that, if I start from scratch and create a new pet, they will give me 30 items back as long as I provide them with the correct item code. 

I must have had almost 300 items in my inventory, all my outfits had been carefully labelled and organized, as well as my house decorations. 

PLEASE don't waste your time on this app, I don't know what they are doing with their data centres but anyone can have their pet deleted at ANY TIME. 

And they will apologize and say there is nothing they can do. Thanks for making me waste countless hours of my life, Finch.

reviews.title: A Cute Idea That Tries a Bit Too Hard
reviews.text:
Finch clearly comes from a good place. The idea of pairing self-care with a little virtual pet is charming on paper, and it’s easy to see why it appeals to some people. Unfortunately, in practice the app leans so hard into “cute” that it becomes twee to the point of being almost condescending.

Everything about Finch — the language, the animations, the tone of encouragement — feels more like it’s aimed at children than adults. Tasks are framed with excessive cheerfulness and overly simplified affirmations, which can make genuine self-reflection feel trivialised. Instead of feeling supported, I often felt talked down to, as though complex emotional states could be fixed with a sticker, a smiley face, and a cartoon bird telling me I’d done great.

For people who already find self-care difficult or awkward, this kind of presentation can be actively off-putting. Rather than lowering the barrier to entry, the saccharine tone risks pushing people away entirely — reinforcing the idea that self-care is fluffy, shallow, or not meant to be taken seriously. Ironically, it’s exactly the sort of approach that can make people bounce off self-care rather than embrace it.

Finch will undoubtedly work well for some users, especially those who enjoy gamified positivity and a very gentle, childlike aesthetic. But for adults looking for something that treats their mental health with a bit more nuance, maturity, and respect, the app may feel more patronising than helpful.

pls fewer newsletters about merch drops and notifications from my pet without any information, and more effective simple, and efficient tools.
